sections.html:
Decide on the type of buyer first. Your options are a financed buyer found through a listing, a buyer you locate yourself, or a cash buyer able to close when you say. With a Census median home value of $339,000 for 2020 to 2024, the price stakes are high, and the three routes can leave you with very different sums.

Wauwatosa is a suburb on the west edge of Milwaukee, in Milwaukee County. Population was estimated at 48,649 in 2025, a small rise from 48,387 in 2020. Your deed will be recorded by the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds.

This is a compact, fully built suburb of about 13 square miles, with older housing. Eastern streets were laid out for a short streetcar ride to downtown Milwaukee, and many homes carry cream-colored brick or limestone foundations. Washington Highlands is a National Register historic district, and flash flooding hit downtown Wauwatosa on August 9 and 10, 2025, which is why buyers may bring up basements. A house near Washington Highlands and a bungalow near the county line will price very differently, because these are citywide medians. The city counts 22,239 households, and owners occupy 60.8 percent of the homes. Median rent is $1,438, median owner costs with a mortgage are $2,071 a month, and median household income stands at $101,138 in 2024 dollars.

A house that needs work gets discounted by an as-is buyer, while a listing buyer is likelier to request fixes after the inspection.

sections.h2: Can unpermitted work hurt a Wauwatosa sale?
sections.html:
Yes. The Building and Safety Division handles this exact situation. If you did work without a permit and the condition report requires you to disclose it, you or your contractor must apply for the missing permit, pay a penalty fee on top of the permit fee, and pass an on-site inspection. Be ready to open finished walls if key work is hidden, and expect to correct any code violations. Depending on the case, the city may also take legal action.

These permit rules come up often on older Wauwatosa homes:

  • A basement bedroom needs a building permit and a second exit, typically an egress window.
  • Replacing a water heater needs a permit, and so do solar installations and underground pipes for downspouts or sump pumps.
  • Front-yard fences need a permit and may not exceed three feet. Side and rear yard fences up to four and a half feet generally do not.
  • Storage sheds over 100 square feet need a permit.
  • New roofing or siding that changes the home's architectural style needs a permit and Design Review Board approval.

Call the division at (414) 479-8913 or the inspector line at (414) 479-8907 before you list. The permit counter at City Hall, 7725 W. North Ave., is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays.

Selling a home of one to four units obliges you to give the buyer a finished real estate condition report. If it is late, the buyer can leave the contract. Wisconsin Statutes chapter 709 allows 10 days from acceptance of the contract. When the 10 days pass, the buyer has two business days to cancel and collect deposits. Fiduciaries of an estate who never lived there do not have to complete it.

The grantor settles a state transfer fee at closing, under Wis. Stat. 77.22, computed at 30 cents for each $100 of value, or $3 for each $1,000. Each party signs the return online, and a deed cannot be accepted until the return is on file.

sections.h2: How assessments and property taxes work in Wauwatosa
sections.html:
Values come from the City Assessor, (414) 479-8969, who neither sets nor collects taxes. Condition on January 1 is what gets assessed. Open Book and Board of Review dates change annually, so call the office before building a plan around them.

DateWhat happens
January 1Assessment date for all property
March 1Deadline for exemption request forms
March 1Deadline for the 2027 Request for Review of Property Assessment
Spring to summerAssessment notices mailed and Open Book review held

The Treasurer's Office collects from December through July 31. By state law, bills are mailed by the third Monday in December to the owner of record shown at the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds, unless the Assessor received a new address before November 15.

sections.h2: When taxes are due and what happens if you owe
sections.html:
You can clear the bill with one payment by January 31 or three interest-free installments on January 31, March 31 and May 31. Being late means 1 percent interest and a 0.5 percent penalty for each month, applied from February 1. After July 31, unpaid taxes go to the Milwaukee County Treasurer at 901 N. 9th Street, (414) 278-4033.

If taxes are still unpaid when you sell, obtain the payoff figure first. At closing, the title company shows how the year's bill is divided.

sections.h2: How is a deed recorded in Milwaukee County?
sections.html:
Record at the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds, 901 N. 9th Street, Room 103. Recording costs $30 and the transfer fee on your return receipt is added. Cards are turned away, so bring cash, a check or a money order. The register works through filings in the order they arrive, which takes three to five business days, and mails originals back within one to two weeks.

Blank deeds and legal advice are not available at the register's office. The deed is usually drafted by a title company or attorney, who also sends the return to the Department of Revenue. Call (414) 278-4005 with recording questions.

sections.h2: Preparing the house and the paperwork
sections.html:
Older Wauwatosa houses reward a seller who comes prepared. Before listing, collect every permit you can find, especially for a basement bedroom, a water heater, solar panels, a fence or an addition. If you did any of that work yourself without a permit, call the inspector before a buyer's inspector brings it up.

Keep the receipts for roofing, siding and any basement water work, and note whether the changes affected the home's architectural style. Open walls are a real possibility if key work is hidden, so a cash buyer who buys as-is can feel simpler than a repair process. Before accepting an offer on any route, have the tax bill and your mortgage payoff figure ready.

sections.h2: What selling options does a Wauwatosa owner have?
sections.html:
Let the house and your target closing date drive the choice.

  • Traditional listing. A well-kept house and an owner who tolerates showings, an inspection and an appraisal make this route work.
  • Sale by owner. Saves on representation but you handle the condition report, contract and disclosures yourself.
  • Cash purchase. Built for houses with open permits, deferred repairs, tenants or an estate waiting to be settled. Get the offer on paper, including who covers title and recording.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for work before selling in Wauwatosa?
faqs.a: It depends on the work. Water heater replacement, solar panels, new basement bedrooms and sheds over 100 square feet need permits. Re-roofing and re-siding generally do not unless they change the home's architectural style. Call the Building and Safety Division at (414) 479-8913 to check.

faqs.q: What happens if I did work without a permit and now want to sell?
faqs.a: You or your contractor must apply for the permit, pay a penalty fee on top of the permit fee, and pass an on-site inspection. Code violations must be corrected first. Discuss your case with the inspector assigned to your district.

faqs.q: When are Wauwatosa property taxes due?
faqs.a: Choose one payment on January 31 or three installments on January 31, March 31 and May 31. Late balances grow by 1 percent in interest and 0.5 percent in penalty each month from February 1. After July 31 the Treasurer stops collecting and unpaid taxes go to the Milwaukee County Treasurer.

faqs.q: What is the Wisconsin transfer fee for a Wauwatosa sale?
faqs.a: The grantor's fee is 30 cents per $100 of value, the equivalent of $3 per $1,000, due at recording. A transfer by will, descent or survivorship is exempt under s. 77.25. Filing of the electronic return is done with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue.

faqs.q: Where is a Wauwatosa deed recorded?
faqs.a: Visit the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds at 901 N. 9th Street. Plan for $30 per document, plus any transfer fee, and bring the electronic return receipt. Most title companies submit the paperwork for you.
